h1: A coding agent your pipeline can trust

pages.text_excerpt:
Headless Agent Harness for Workflow Automation | aictrl.dev MIT-licensed headless agent harness A coding agent your pipeline can trust A repeatable agent harness: minimal, fast and safe. TL;DR Agents built for a terminal hang on prompts nobody can answer, exit 0 when they failed and bury the answer in prose. aictrl CLI rejects permission prompts instead of waiting, streams versioned JSON events, checks the result against your schema and exits with a code your pipeline can act on. npm i -g @aictrl/cli The CLI is free under MIT. Model usage is billed separately by your provider. Read the Benchmark GitHub Actions Terminal Ask your agent name: aictrl review

on:
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize, ready_for_review]

permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write

concurrency:
  group: aictrl-review-${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  review:
    # Fork pull requests get no secrets; never switch this to pull_request_target.
    if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository && !github.event.pull_request.draft
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    env:
      PR: ${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
        with:
          persist-credentials: false

      # 1. Fetch the diff with the GitHub token. The model key is not in this step.
      - run: gh pr diff "$PR" > pr.diff
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}

      - run: npm install -g @aictrl/cli@0.5.4

      # 0.5.4 still loads AGENTS.md with project config disabled (aictrl-dev/cli#250),
      # so delete them from this throwaway checkout before the model step.
      - run: find . -name AGENTS.md -not -path './.git/*' -delete

      # 2. Review with the model key only: no GitHub token, no shell, read-only tools,
      #    no .aictrl config and no AGENTS.md from the pull request.
      - name: Review
        env:
          # Only the key for your provider, from a repository secret.
          ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
          # Repository variable in provider/model form.
          MODEL: ${{ vars.AICTRL_MODEL }}
          AICTRL_DISABLE_PROJECT_CONFIG: "true"
          AICTRL_MODEL_STREAM_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS: "300000"
          AICTRL_CONFIG_CONTENT: >-
            {"permission": {"*": "deny", "read": "allow", "glob": "allow", "grep": "allow"}}
        run: |
          aictrl run --format json --model "$MODEL" \
            "Review the change in pr.diff. Read files in this repository for context.
          Report bugs, security and reliability problems with file and line; skip style.
          Reply with the review only, in Markdown." < /dev/null > aictrl-events.jsonl
          jq -rs '[.[] | select(.type == "text") | .part.text] | last // empty' aictrl-events.jsonl > review.md
          test -s review.md

      # 3. Post with the GitHub token. The model key is not in this step.
      - run: gh pr comment "$PR" --body-file review.md --edit-last --create-if-none
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}

      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with:
          name: aictrl-events
          path: aictrl-events.jsonl
          retention-days: 7 Save as .github/workflows/aictrl-review.yml , add your provider's API key as a repository secret and set the AICTRL_MODEL repository variable, for example anthropic/<model> . No step holds both the model key and a way to post: the agent gets the key but no GitHub token and no shell, and only the posting step can write to the pull request. The AGENTS.md step stays until a release fixes cli#250 . npm i -g @aictrl/cli
# Anthropic here; for another provider, check its key variable.
: "${ANTHROPIC_API_KEY:?export your key}"

# Read-only, plus the agent's draft file. Stalled stream: 5 min.
export AICTRL_DISABLE_PROJECT_CONFIG=true
export AICTRL_MODEL_STREAM_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS=300000
export AICTRL_CONFIG_CONTENT='{"permission": {"*": "deny", "read": "allow", "glob": "allow", "grep": "allow", "edit": {"*": "deny", "draft.json": "allow"}}}'

cat > findings.schema.json <<'JSON'
{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "findings": { "type": "array", "items": { "type": "string" } }
  },
  "required": ["findings"],
  "additionalProperties": false
}
JSON

timeout --kill-after=30s 15m aictrl run --format json \
  --model anthropic/MODEL_ID \
  --output-schema findings.schema.json \
  --output-result findings.json \
  "Review this repository for security and reliability bugs. Write the findings to draft.json." \
  < /dev/null > aictrl-events.jsonl For another provider, check its key variable instead and pass its model to --model . The agent can read the repository and write only draft.json ; the CLI writes findings.json once the draft passes the schema. timeout (GNU coreutils) caps the run. In a repository you don't trust, delete AGENTS.md files first, as the GitHub Actions tab does. Add a GitHub Actions workflow to this repository that reviews every pull request with aictrl CLI (npm package @aictrl/cli; overview at https://aictrl.dev/agent). Keep the model key and the GitHub token in separate steps:

1. With the GitHub token only: write the pull request diff to pr.diff with gh pr diff.
2. Install a pinned @aictrl/cli version, then delete every AGENTS.md in the checkout with find . -name AGENTS.md -not -path './.git/*' -delete (until https://github.com/aictrl-dev/cli/issues/250 is fixed in a release). With the model API key only (no GitHub token), run aictrl run --format json --model <provider/model> with unused stdin closed using < /dev/null. Set AICTRL_DISABLE_PROJECT_CONFIG=true, AICTRL_MODEL_STREAM_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS=300000 and AICTRL_CONFIG_CONTENT to deny every tool except read, glob and grep. Ask for bugs, security and reliability problems with file and line, no style comments, and the review only, in Markdown. Take the last text event from the JSON output as the review.
3. With the GitHub token only: post the review with gh pr comment --edit-last --create-if-none.

Run on pull_request (never pull_request_target) for same-repository branches, with contents: read and pull-requests: write, a concurrency group per pull request and a 15-minute timeout. PR ingestion and lifecycle Track opened, reviewed, and merged pull requests with repository, branch, author, review run, and finding state attached to the PR record. Tool-enabled review agents Agents can use repository context, knowledge graph links, product docs, review policy, test evidence, and static-analysis signals instead of commenting from the diff alone. Actionable finding workflow Findings carry severity, file, line, status, and triage state so teams can separate true positives from noise and escalate work into issues. Review quality analytics Measure total findings, actionability rate, review duration, noisy rules, and PR funnel movement instead of counting bot comments. Team learning loops Use false-positive concentration and accepted findings to tune review skills, repository instructions, and rule sets over time. Delivery metric linkage Connect review adoption to DORA-adjacent signals such as lead time, change failure rate, MTTR, turnaround time, and rework. Rendered review UX The PR comment is part of the product. aictrl-bot uses GitHub and GitLab markdown as an execution surface: line-local findings, code spans, collapsible evidence, diagrams, task links, and agent handoff prompts. That makes the review easier to verify than a paragraph generated from the diff alone. Tool-enabled evidence The agent can use repository search, knowledge graph context, product docs, and policy instructions before it writes a finding. Actionable handoff Findings can link to fix tasks, IDE handoff prompts, documentation, or follow-up workflows instead of stopping at a comment. pages.text_excerpt: Which coding-agent CLI is best for headless workflow automation? | aictrl.dev ai ctrl .dev Blog Research / Headless agents Which coding-agent CLI is best for headless workflow automation? Bulat · Co-authored with AI · 21 October 2026 A coding-agent CLI can feel quick in a terminal and still be expensive when a workflow starts it in a fresh container for every job. We measured that cost for six CLIs: start-up, time per turn, memory, image size and tokens. On overhead per job, pi was the lightest overall. Our own CLI, aictrl , won no metric but came second on four: session time, harness time per turn, memory and image size. Overhead is half the answer: this experiment does not measure whether an agent completes the task, which our next run will. Goose had the fastest observed median first response, followed by Codex, pi and aictrl. Those four were within 187 ms of each other. pi used the fewest tokens, both in its first request and for a whole short task, spent the least time between model turns, added the least image footprint and finished the scripted session fastest. aictrl came second on session time, per-turn harness time, memory and image footprint. Its system prompt is now as small as pi's. Its tool definitions are not. Each chart is sorted from lowest to highest, with gold and silver medals for the observed first and second place on that metric. A medal describes this experiment; small gaps do not establish a stable lead. Disclosure: I build aictrl. This article reports our own measurements, including where our implementation loses. The article and charts were prepared with AI assistance. What we measured Fresh 2-CPU containers, a local 50 ms scripted model, six released CLIs with different toolsets. On 20 October 2026 we tested released installations of aictrl 0.5.4, pi 1.3.0, Codex 0.163.0, OpenCode 2.1.0, Hermes Agent v0.22.2 source and Goose 1.55.0. Hermes' source archive reports vunknown ; we identify it by its pinned release commit in the methodology . Every attempt started a fresh non-root container with an empty home directory, a two-CPU quota and a 2 GiB memory limit. Images were already on the host, and filesystem caches were not cleared. These are fresh-container measurements, excluding image downloads and cloud scheduling. A local scripted model responded after a fixed 50 ms delay. It removed remote inference variability and dictated the reads. This tests harness overhead and native tool execution; it cannot measure coding quality or natural model-turn efficiency. We collected 20 measured single-response attempts per harness and five attempts for the 50-read memory task, with two discarded warmups per scenario and interleaved harness order. All six used their own native tool loops. Hermes did not delegate to Codex, and Goose did not delegate through ACP. Every attempt completed, and the runner recorded no failures. The toolsets were not equal, and that matters most for the token results. pi ran with its four default tools, no subagent tool and no extensions or packages installed. Goose ran with only its built-in Developer extension, so no recipes or sub-recipes were loaded. Hermes ran with only its file and terminal toolsets; its default also enables web, browser, memory and task delegation, among others. aictrl, OpenCode and Codex ran with their default tools, which include a subagent tool in each. The section on tokens adds aictrl restricted to pi's four tools. Each harness ran non-interactively with its JSON output on. Besides the scripted model's provider settings, the flags were: aictrl: aictrl run --format json pi: pi --mode json Codex: codex exec --json --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox --skip-git-repo-check OpenCode: opencode run --standalone --auto --format json Goose: goose run --no-profile --with-builtin developer --output-format stream-json Hermes: hermes chat --oneshot --toolsets file,terminal --ignore-user-config --ignore-rules --format stream-json The runner has the full adapters, environment and config files. For token counts we ran a separate capture campaign with the same images and setup. It used five single-response and five 50-read sessions per harness and retained every request body. We counted every harness with one reference tokenizer, OpenAI's o200k_base . These are estimates of what each harness sends, not provider-billed usage. The measurement extract , token estimates , CSV and methodology accompany the figures. Memory and footprint use MiB; request bodies use actual UTF-8 bytes. Select any chart to open the full-resolution image. Goose had the fastest observed median first response The timer started immediately before docker run and stopped at the first matching assistant-response event in the harness's JSON output. Container startup and our setup wrapper count. This is not model time to first token. Figure 1. Source: our six-harness fresh-container measurements, 20 October 2026; 20 attempts each. The connecting lines are not confidence intervals. Goose reached the first response in 392 ms at the median, followed by Codex at 471, pi at 522 and aictrl at 579. With 20 samples on a shared host, I would not claim a repeatable ordering among those four. Absolute startup times also moved between our campaigns: the same Goose, Codex, pi and Hermes images measured 140 to 230 ms faster on 20 October than a day earlier. A separate paired run of aictrl and pi measured 503 and 460 ms. Compare startup times within one campaign only. OpenCode 2.1.0 took 926 ms and Hermes 5.5 s, gaps that warrant profiling under the same setup. These are supported installation profiles with different runtimes, dependencies and startup behavior. pi used Node 22; Hermes core used Python 3.14.8. The other three npm installations used a Node 20 base, while packaged native executables can carry their own runtime. Those differences prevent attributing the result to a programming language. Memory depends on what reaches the next model request The long task read fifty distinct files containing the same 48,000-byte, 800-line fixture, then answered Done. . Distinct paths matter: Hermes normally deduplicates unchanged reads. We preserved that behavior while asking each harness to do actual reads of equal-sized files. Figure 2. Source: our six-harness measurements, 20 October 2026. Five attempts per harness; completed-run counts and RSS are in the CSV. At five completed runs, nearest-rank p90 is the maximum. Codex is listed last without a medal: it keeps only the fi
